antibiotic resistance genes of cattle manure anaerobic digestion by air 
nanobubble water

Keywords:

A B S T R A C T
The excessive use of antibiotics in livestock farming has made cattle manure (CM) a reservoir for antibiotic 
resistance genes (ARGs). Anaerobic digestion (AD) can mitigate the risk of spreading ARGs, but its treatment 
capacity has limitations. This study investigated the effect of air nanobubble water (Air-NBW) on methano­
genesis performance and ARGs dynamics during mesophilic and psychrotrophic AD of CM. The results show that 
Air-NBW enhanced cumulative methane production by 43.4% (mesophilic) and 50.2% (psychrotrophic) by 
upregulating key functional genes involved in hydrogenotrophic and acetoclastic methanogenesis. Gompertz 
fitting further showed that the maximum methane yield rate increased by over 62.2% under both temperature 
conditions. Under mesophilic conditions, Air-NBW had a greater impact on the abundance of mobile genetic 
elements and the expression of ARG transfer genes than under psychrotrophic conditions. Specifically, Air-NBW 
led to a 50.7% decrease in mobile genetic elements, a 39.6% downregulation in biofilm-related genes, and a 
24.5% upregulation in antioxidant genes, along with a reduction in ARG abundance. This suggests Air-NBW 
helps lower overall ARG levels. Meanwhile, Air-NBW reduced the abundance of specific ARGs (lnu(D), lsa(B),

1. Introduction
China's livestock industry ranks among the world's largest, gener­
ating approximately 1.38 billion tonnes of cattle manure (CM) annually 
(Zhang et al., 2025). The prolonged excessive use of antibiotics during 
livestock farming has resulted in the appearance of antibiotic resistance 
genes (ARGs), and the agricultural application of manure further ac­
celerates the environmental spread of ARGs (Liu et al., 2025). ARGs can 
spread across species through horizontal gene transfer (HGT) facilitated 
by mobile genetic elements (MGEs), thereby escalating ecological and 
health risks (Haffiez et al., 2022). By 2050, antibiotic resistance annual 
deaths worldwide are projected to exceed 10 million (Peng et al., 2025).
Anaerobic digestion (AD) can stably process CM, produce methane, 
and efficiently convert CM into agricultural fertilizer (He et al., 2025). 
However, AD may have limited impact on reducing ARGs (Haffiez et al., 
2022). During the mesophilic AD of CM, the absolute abundance of 12 
ARGs decreased, including ermF (Macrolide-lincosamide-streptogramin 
(MLS) type ARGs), tetW (tetracycline type ARGs) and sul2 (Ma et al., 
2019). However, tetM and tetQ exhibited enrichment under mesophilic 
and psychrotrophic conditions, while sul1 exhibited enrichment only 
under psychrotrophic conditions during the AD of CM (Sun et al., 2016).
Air nanobubble water (Air-NBW) offers the advantages of simple 
preparation, low cost, and environmental friendliness (Zhang et al., 
2024). Air-NBW contains abundant nanobubbles with diameters < 1 μm, 
which, owing to their high specific surface area, long residence time, and 
relatively high interfacial charge, can effectively enhance gas dissolu­
tion and mass transfer (Bian et al., 2026). This characteristic can pro­
mote the hydrolysis of macromolecular organic compounds and further 
enhance hydrolysis efficiency by creating micro-aerobic environments, 
optimizing electron transfer, and enriching facultative anaerobic bac­
teria (Chuenchart et al., 2021). As a result regulates the production and 
composition of volatile fatty acid (VFAs), mitigates the risk of acid 
accumulation, enhances system stability, and ultimately increases 
methane production (Hou et al., 2025). Additionally, Air-NBW can 
scavenge reactive oxygen species (ROS) by enhancing the activity and 
gene expression of antioxidant enzymes such as glutathione peroxidase, 
superoxide dismutase, and catalase (Zhang et al., 2022).
In sludge AD, Air-NBW increased methane production in the anaer­
obic digestion process, with the 40.0% NBW group showing a 16.0% 
increase in methane yield, likely due to the promotion of the hydrolysis 
stage, increased VFA accumulation, and the enhancement of the mi­
crobial growth environment through nanobubbles (Wang et al., 2025). 
During corn stover AD, Air-NBW enhanced methane production by 
11.9% to 24.1% through promoting microbial growth for lignocellulose 
degradation, improving hydrolysis efficiency, and stabilizing the 
anaerobic environment via enhanced mass transfer (Bian et al., 2026). 
During the mesophilic AD of CM, Air-NBW increased the abundance of 
key hydrolytic bacteria (Bacillus) and mixotrophic methanogens (Meth­
anosarcina) from 0.3% and 20.3% to 39.2% and 47.4%, respectively, and 
cumulative methane production by 9.7% (Zhang et al., 2024). While 
substantial evidence supports the positive effect of Air-NBW on methane 
production in various AD systems, little to no research has been con­
ducted on its impact on ARGs.
The reductive effect of NBW on ARGs results from the combined 
effects of substrate environment changes, genetic material transfer, and 
community restructuring. Air-NBW may promote hydrolysis and 
methane production under mildly aerobic conditions or redox regula­
tion, potentially reducing VFA accumulation, restructuring the 
anaerobic system, and weakening the competitive advantage of high 
ARG bacteria, which could, in turn, alleviate ROS-related stress re­
sponses and HGT (Chuenchart et al., 2021; Feng et al., 2025). Biofilm 
facilitates the HGT of ARGs through MGEs such as plasmids and inte­
grons, making them recognized hotspots for ARG dissemination 
(Michaelis & Grohmann, 2023). NBW may disrupt the biofilm matrix, 
which is primarily composed of extracellular polymeric substances 
(EPS), through nano-scale gas–liquid interface effects, thereby affecting 
its stability (Kobayashi et al., 2025). Given the critical role of EPS in cell 
adhesion, aggregation, and biofilm stability, the disruption of EPS and 
biofilm by NBW could reduce cell aggregation, leading to changes in 
community structure (Wang et al., 2024). These microbial composition 
changes may impact the abundance and host range of ARGs and MGEs, 
ultimately reshaping the antibiotic resistance gene profile (Michaelis & 
Grohmann, 2023). Specifically, the effects of Air-NBW on the abundance 
of MGEs, the expression of functional genes related to biofilm formation, 
antioxidative defense, DNA repair and recombination, and the type IV 
secretion system remain unclear. Furthermore, the potential links be­
tween these factors and the HGT of ARGs are not well understood. 
Additionally, the role of Air-NBW in attenuating ARGs and mitigating 
ecological risks has been largely overlooked.
This study investigates the effects of adding Air-NBW on system 
performance during mesophilic and psychrotrophic AD of CM. Further 
analysis examined the regulatory role of Air-NBW in ARGs transfer, 
degradation, and ecological risk.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
CM was collected from a standardized dairy farm in Lanzhou, China, 
and stored at 4 ◦C. The median particle size (D50) of the CM was 33.1 μm 
(Fig. S1). Seed sludge for each digester was waste activated sludge pre- 
digested anaerobically for 10 days under either mesophilic (37 ± 1 ◦C) 
or psychrotrophic (25 ± 1 ◦C) conditions. Air-NBW was prepared by 
injecting air into distilled water (0.4–0.5 MPa, 20 min, 20 ◦C) using a 
nanobubble generator (JXWNP-AL01, Jinxiang, China) with continuous 
recirculation. Fresh NBW appeared milky white and became clear within 
5–10 min as larger bubbles rose and dissipated. The physicochemical 
characteristics of CM and digested sludge (Table S1), as well as the basic 
properties of Air-NBW, are provided in Table S2 and Fig. S2.
2.2. Experimental setup
In each digester, CM was mixed with the water (Air-NBW or distilled 
water) at a 1:1 mass ratio with a total mass of 1200 g (Zhang et al., 
2024). Each digester was then inoculated with 150 g of anaerobic 
digested sludge, establishing the initial substrate (IS). The inoculum-to- 
substrate ratio (ISR) and initial substrate concentration on a volatile 
solids (VS) basis (C0, VS) were 4.8 × 10-2 and 55.9 ± 0.7 g VS/L, 
respectively (mesophilic), and 5.3 × 10-2 and 56.2 ± 0.7 g VS/L, 
respectively (psychrotrophic). Batch experiments were run under mes­
ophilic or psychrotrophic conditions, using NBW as the treatment and 
distilled water as the control, yielding four groups: the mesophilic 
nanobubble water group (MN), the mesophilic distilled water group 
(MD), the psychrotrophic nanobubble water group (PN), and the psy­
chrotrophic distilled water group (PD). Each of the four experimental 
conditions (MN, MD, PN, and PD) was set up in three parallel replicates.

A 2 L bottle reactor was sealed with a custom lid fitted with two 4 
mm metal tubes connected to silicone hoses. One tube was connected to 
a gas collection bag for biogas storage, and the other was used to 
withdraw digestate via a peristaltic pump. The reactor was shaken for 1 
min daily for mixing. Digestate was sampled on days 0 and 3, then every 
7 days until day 49.
2.3. Anaerobic digestion analysis methods
Uniformly mixed samples were collected regularly from each 
digester, centrifuged, and filtered through PES membrane with a 0.45 
μm aperture, yielding the filtrate. Total solids (TS) and volatile solids 
(VS) were analyzed from the original samples of cattle manure and 
digested sludge, while pH, soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD), 
and total ammonia nitrogen (TAN) were measured from the filtrate, all 
according to standard methods (APHA, 1999). Free ammonia nitrogen 
(FAN) was calculated using Hansen’s formula (Hansen et al., 1998). 
VFAs and methane content of biogas were determined using a gas 
chromatography (7890Plus, Ruihong, China). The biogas volume was 
determined by a gas flow meter (LMI-2, Alpha, China). Elemental 
composition (C, H, N, S) was determined using an organic elemental 
analyzer (Vario EL Cube, Elementar, Germany).
2.4. Microbiome and macrogenetic analysis
Sample DNA was extracted using the HiPure Soil DNA kit at pre­
determined time points and analyzed the 16S rDNA gene through high- 
throughput sequencing. Bacterial and archaea amplification was per­
formed using primer sets (341F: CCTACGGGNGGCWGCAG and 806R: 
GGACTACHVGGGGTATCTAAT) and (Arch519F: CAGCMGCCGCGG­
TAA and Arch915R: GTGCTCCCCCGCCAATTCCT), respectively. The 
resulting amplicons were subjected to paired-end sequencing on the 
Illumina PE250 platform, followed by comprehensive bioinformatic 
processing.
Metagenomic sequencing using the Illumina NovaSeq platform, 
combined with bioinformatics analysis, was used to compare functional 
gene profiles of samples on day 0, day 21, and day 49 (Methods S1) 
(P¨arn¨anen et al., 2018; Yin et al., 2023). Ecological risk scores (ERS) 
were calculated using the MetaCompare 2.0 framework to assess anti­
biotic resistance risk. Metagenomic reads were assembled into contigs, 
annotated for ARGs, MGEs, and host taxonomy, and the co-localization 
of ARGs with MGEs and pathogenic hosts was identified. Abundances 
were normalized based on contig counts. Finally, samples were pro­
jected into a hazard space to derive and rank resistome risk scores (Rumi 
et al., 2024).
2.5. Data analysis
Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS 27.0 (Windows 
version). Differences between experimental groups were compared via 
one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) (significance threshold p <
0.05). All data are expressed as mean ± standard deviation. The cu­
mulative methane production data were fitted using the modified 
Gompertz equation, and the model parameters were estimated by 
nonlinear least-squares regression (Methods S2) (Dhamodharan et al., 
2015).
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Anaerobic digestion performance and methane yield
3.1.1. pH, SCOD, TAN, FAN and VFAs
AD relies on maintaining pH within an optimal range to support 
microbial growth and metabolic activity, thereby ensuring process sta­
bility and efficiency (Chen et al., 2022). The pH dropped to its lowest 
point on day 3 (mesophilic) and day 7 (psychrotrophic) (Fig. 1a). It

subsequently rebounded, reaching a peak before experiencing a second 
decline on day 35. The initial pH drop was associated with the accu­
mulation of VFAs, which peaked on day 3 and day 7, respectively 
(Fig. S3) (Bian et al., 2026). Subsequently, ammoniacal nitrogen 
contributed partial alkalinity and buffering capacity, mitigating VFA 
accumulation and maintaining the reactor pH within a mildly alkaline to 
neutral range (Li et al., 2024).
SCOD peaked on day 3 (mesophilic) and day 7 (psychrotrophic), 
with higher values observed in the NBW group compared with the 
control, followed by a gradual decline (Fig. 1b). SCOD variations reflect 
hydrolysis-driven VFA production (Bian et al., 2026). The syntrophic 
oxidation of propionate and butyrate is thermodynamically constrained, 
requiring extremely low hydrogen or formate partial pressures (Lv et al., 
2020). Air-NBW-induced microaerophilic conditions stimulate faculta­
tive anaerobes to scavenge oxygen and maintain redox balance, thereby 
alleviating thermodynamic limitations (Chuenchart et al., 2021). This 
enhances syntrophic cooperation, electron transfer, and accelerates VFA 
conversion, contributing to higher SCOD peaks. The subsequent decline 
in SCOD is attributed to the consumption of organic acids by meth­
anogenic archaea, which convert them into methane (Zhang et al., 
2024).
TAN is a product of the degradation of nitrogenous organic matter in 
AD (Gao et al., 2023). TAN exhibited an increasing trend across all 
groups, with higher levels in the NBW group compared to the corre­
sponding control under both temperature conditions (Fig. 1c). Air-NBW 
enhanced substrate hydrolysis and microbial activity, accelerating the 
degradation of organic nitrogen in cow manure and increasing TAN 
levels, with total concentrations remaining below 1500 mg L−1, which is 
within a suitable range for microbial use (Peng et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 
2024). FAN showed an initial increase followed by a decrease, peaking 
on day 35 (Fig. 1d). The effect of Air-NBW on FAN mirrored its influence 
on pH. Under alkaline conditions, ammonia primarily exists as free 
ammonia, and changes in water pH directly affect the balance between 
ammonia and ammonium ions. FAN remained below 200  mg L−1 in all 
treatments and did not significantly affect methane production (Zhang 
et al., 2024).
3.1.2. Methane yield
Daily methane production rate is a key indicator for evaluating 
anaerobic digestion efficiency (Chen et al., 2022). It exhibited two peaks 
under both temperature conditions, with higher values observed in the 
NBW group compared with the corresponding controls (Fig. 1e). The 
first peak occurred on day 3 (mesophilic) and day 7 (psychrotrophic), 
while the second peak was observed on days 21 and 35, respectively, 
followed by a gradual decline after each peak. During the initial phase, 
Air-NBW may boost AD start-up by transiently creating a micro­
aerophilic niche that speeds oxygen removal and strict anaerobiosis, 
improves mass transfer and hydrolysis, and may promote syntrophy 
mediated by direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET), thereby 
reducing VFA accumulation and increasing methane yield (Bian et al., 
2026; Chuenchart et al., 2021; Lv et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2024). At the 
VFA peak, acetate predominated, indicating substrate accumulation 
toward subsequent methanogenesis (Fig. S3) (Bian et al., 2026). Sub­
sequently, propionate exceeded acetate and became the primary inhib­
itor of methane production due to limited conversion, leading to a 
gradual decline in daily methane yield (Fu et al., 2020). On day 21 under 
mesophilic conditions, Bacillota and Bacteroidota predominated, with a 
larger increase in Bacteroidota in MN than in MD (Fig. S4a). Bacteroidota 
shows strong cellulose-degrading capacity during AD, likely due to its 
electroactivity and higher glycolytic enzyme activity than Bacillota (Sha 
et al., 2023). On day 35 under psychrotrophic conditions, the relative 
abundance of Methanosarcina in PN was higher than in PD (Fig. S4b). 
Methanosarcina can accelerate VFAs utilization and methane synthesis 
through interspecies DIET (Liu et al., 2023). Air-NBW may enhance the 
recovery phase by reducing H2 and formate diffusion limitations and 
promoting DIET, thereby improving VFAs utilization and methane 
performance during recovery (Akram et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2020). 
Accordingly, cumulative methane production was higher in MN than in 
MD, and in PN than in PD, by 43.4% and 50.2%, respectively (Fig. 1f).
The Gompertz model provided a good fit to the cumulative methane 
production profiles (Table 1). Rm (maximum methane yield rate) and 
UMP (ultimate methane production) can both be used to characterize 
methane production performance in AD, with Rm reflecting the methane 
production rate and kinetic characteristics of the system and UMP rep­
resenting its ultimate methane production potential (Lee et al., 2024). In 
the NBW group, both Rm and UMP were significantly higher than those 
in the corresponding control groups (p < 0.05). These results suggest 
that Air-NBW may enrich hydrolytic-acidogenic bacteria and syntrophs, 
enhancing H2 and formate transfer within flocs to ease thermodynamic 
constraints and boost methanogenic synergy (Akram et al., 2024; Hou 
et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024). The magnitude of the λ directly reflects 
the speed at which microorganisms mount an effective response to 
environmental stress. A higher λ prolongs the activation time of mi­
crobial enzyme systems and the degradation cycle of environmental 
inhibitory substances, thereby delaying the exponential growth phase 
and postponing the initiation of methane production (Fu et al., 2020). 
Air-NBW shortened λ under mesophilic conditions, yet lengthened λ 
under psychrotrophic conditions. Under mesophilic conditions, Air- 
NBW may significantly enhance the degradation of macromolecular 
organic compounds by strengthening the electron transport system and 
optimizing the catalytic efficiency of enzymes associated with hydrolysis 
and acid production (Bian et al., 2026). However, under psychrotrophic 
conditions, anaerobic microorganisms exhibit inherently low activity, 
and adding Air-NBW further alters the internal environment of the 
digester, thus requiring them to undergo an adaptation period (Wang 
et al., 2020). In summary, Air-NBW significantly enhanced methano­
genesis performance during mesophilic and psychrotrophic AD of CM.
3.2. Bacterial and archaeal communities and methanogenic pathways
At the phylum level of bacterial communities, Bacillota, Bacteroidota, 
Spirochaetota, Chloroflexota, and Synergistota were the key phyla domi­
nating lignocellulose polymer degradation and fermentation processes 
across all groups (Fig. 2a) (Lu et al., 2022). On day 21, Air-NBW 
increased the overall relative abundance of these five phyla under 
mesophilic conditions, from 54.1% in MD to 54.6% in MN. This change 
suggests accelerated organic matter breakdown via enrichment of hy­
drolytic bacteria and consequently enhanced conversion to VFAs and 
methane (Figs. S3 and 1f) (Hou et al., 2025). In contrast, under psy­
chrotrophic conditions, Air-NBW reduced their combined abundance 
relative to the corresponding control, consistent with the delayed onset 
of gas production. On day 49, the NBW group showed a higher combined

control under both temperature conditions, rising from 49.0% in MD to 
50.8% in MN (mesophilic) and from 55.2% in PD to 56.5% in PN 
(psychrotrophic). Genus-level analysis identified Clostridium as domi­
nant. Under mesophilic conditions, it rapidly converts complex organics 
into VFAs, H2 and CO2 to support methanogenesis, whereas under psy­
chrotrophic conditions, conversion is slower due to reduced enzymatic 
and metabolic activity, often requiring acclimation and longer retention 
time or lower loading for stability (Nie et al., 2021). Further genus-level 
analysis revealed that the NBW group exhibited higher relative abun­
dances of taxa classified as “Others” and “unclassified,” alongside an 
elevated Chao1 index (Fig. 2b and S5). The addition of Air-NBW 
increased microbial richness and community complexity, potentially 
through enhanced syntrophic interactions and community restructuring 
(Hou et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024). These results suggest that Air- 
NBW may promote the enrichment of the key phyla dominating ligno­
cellulose polymer degradation and fermentation during AD, thereby 
enhancing the hydrolysis and acidification of organic matter. This 
facilitated increased VFAs production and supplied more substrates for 
methanogenesis, ultimately leading to higher methane yields in the 
NBW group compared with the corresponding control.
At the phylum level of archaeal communities, Euryarchaeota 
(67.6–80.1%) exhibited overwhelmingly dominated (Fig. 2c). This 
phylum primarily comprises hydrogenotrophic methanogens (Meth­
anobrevibacter, Methanocorpusculum, Methanoculleus, Methanospirillum, 
Methanofollis, Methanosphaerula and Methanobacterium), acetoclastic 
methanogens (Methanothrix), and mixotrophic methanogens (Meth­
anosarcina) (Fig. 2d) (Bian et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2025). Meth­
anoculleus is a hydrogenotrophic methanogen that reduces CO2 with H2 
to keep H2 partial pressure low and sustain syntrophic methane forma­
tion, while Methanothrix is more competitive at low acetate concen­
trations (Kakuk et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2026). Temperature strongly 
regulates methanogenesis: mesophilic conditions boost Methanoculleus 
activity and biogas yield, whereas psychrotrophic conditions slow start- 
up and methane production, favoring Methanothrix at low acetate 
(Rama et al., 2024). At the genus level, on day 21, the persistent pres­
ence of Air-NBW may have created a micro-oxic niche that favored 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens capable of remaining metabolically 
active under harsh conditions, thus gaining a competitive advantage 
(Peng et al., 2025). Accordingly, their relative abundance increased 
from 41.4% in MD to 43.7% in MN and from 43.6% in PD to 46.5% in 
PN. By day 30, the system had entered a strictly anaerobic state; as 
oxygen was depleted, the microbial community gradually became 
dominated by acetoclastic methanogens (Chuenchart et al., 2025). On 
day 49, their relative abundance increased from 11.1% in MD to 14.6% 
in MN, and from 8.6% in PD to 12.3% in PN.
The methanogenesis pathways in the AD system is primarily domi­
nated by hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis (M00567) and acetoclastic 
methanogenesis (M00357) (Fig. 2e) (Gao et al., 2023). The ratio of 
homoacetogenesis to combined hydrogenotrophic and acetoclastic 
methanogenesis ranged from 19.3% to 25.3%, consistently below 
25.5%, indicating a limited contribution. NBW showed notable differ­
ences under mesophilic conditions but minimal variation under psy­
chrotrophic conditions. Under both temperature conditions, adding Air- 
NBW induced the upregulation of functional genes associated with the 
hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis pathway (Fig. 2f). Compared with 
PD, PN showed higher hmd expression (log2FC = 5.7 × 10-1), while 
compared with MD, ftr expression was higher in MN (log2FC = 3.9 × 10- 
1). This may be due to Air-NBW enriching the key hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens Methanocorpusculum and Methanobrevibacter under psy­
chrotrophic and mesophilic conditions, respectively, thereby enhancing 
their utilization of H2 and CO2, promoting a mutualistic relationship 
with fermentative bacteria, alleviating product inhibition, and thus 
facilitating methane production in the system (Rama et al., 2024). In the 
acetoclastic methanogenesis pathway, the cdhC (log2(FC) = 5.7 × 10-1) 
and cdhE (log2(FC) = 3.5 × 10-1) gene in MN showed higher expression 
levels compared with MD. This is consistent with the earlier observation 
that acetate production was higher in MN than in MD (Fig. S3a and S3b).

acetate (Hou et al., 2025). Under psychrotrophic conditions, cdhC gene 
expression was significantly downregulated in PN compared with PD. In 
VFA-limited environments, microbial communities allocate resources 
toward the hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis pathway, which offers 
higher energy returns (Liu et al., 2020). Air-NBW increased the pro­
portion of hydrogenotrophic methanogen on day 21 (Fig. 2d). There­
fore, daily methane production rate by PN is greater than that of PD 
(Fig. 1e).
Overall, under psychrotrophic conditions, Air-NBW primarily pro­
motes the hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis pathway, whereas under 
mesophilic conditions, both hydrogenotrophic and acetoclastic meth­
anogenesis pathways are enhanced. This temperature-dependent mod­
ulation of methanogenic pathways directs metabolic fluxes toward the 
energetically favorable pathways in each environment, thereby facili­
tating more efficient methane production.
3.3. Changes in antibiotic resistance genes and mobile genetic elements
MLS and tetracycline ARGs were predominant in the AD system of 
CM (Fig. 3a and S6). The NBW group showed a reduction in the total 
number of ARGs by 0.1% (mesophilic) and 4.1% (psychrotrophic) on 
day 49 compared with the corresponding control group. For MLS and 
tetracycline types ARGs, Air-NBW suppressed the abundance of lnu(D), 
lsa(B), mph(B), tet(W), tet(T), and tet(Q) under both temperature con­
ditions on days 21 and 49 (Fig. 3b and 3c). The reductions in the six 
genes were approximately 5.1–15.6%, 0.0–13.7%, 14.2–73.6%, 
1.2–14.0%, 13.0–41.5% and 4.9–49.2%, respectively. Tet(W), tet(T), 
and tet(Q) belong to the ribosomal protection proteins gene family 
mediating tetracycline resistance in Gram-positive bacteria (Zhanel 
et al., 2016). The relative abundance of Gram-positive bacteria in the 
NBW group was lower than that in the corresponding control group. Lnu 
(D), mph(B) and tet(T) showed significant negative correlations with the 
concentration of acetic acid and propionic acid (p < 0.05), with the 
following correlation coefficients: Lnu(D) (acetic acid −6.5 × 10-1, 
propionic acid −6.1 × 10-1), mph(B) (acetic acid −6.8 × 10-1, propionic 
acid −6.7 × 10-1), and tet(T) (acetic acid −6.1 × 10-1, propionic acid 
−5.9 × 10-1) (Fig. S7a and S7c). Despite the stage-dependent con­
sumption of VFAs, Air-NBW still showed a clear promoting effect on 
VFAs production (Fig. S3). In line with this, lsa(B) and tet(W) exhibited 
significant negative correlations with TAN and FAN, with correlation 
coefficients as follows: lsa(B) (TAN −7.1 × 10-1 (p < 0.01), FAN −7.1 ×
10-1 (p < 0.05)), and tet(W) (TAN −8.4 × 10-1, FAN −9.2 × 10-1) (p <
0.001) (Fig. S7a and S7c). Additionally, Lnu(D) and tet(Q) showed sig­
nificant negative correlations with the bacterial phyla Pseudomonadota 
and Actinomycetota, with correlation coefficients as follows: Lnu(D) 
(Pseudomonadota −8.0 × 10-1, Actinomycetota −7.7 × 10-1) (p < 0.01), 
and tet(Q) (Pseudomonadota −8.3 × 10-1 (p < 0.001), Actinomycetota 
−5.9 × 10-1 (p < 0.05)) (Fig. S7b and S7d). Air-NBW increased the total 
abundance of Pseudomonadota and Actinomycetota, two phyla possessing 
hydrolytic capabilities (Peng et al., 2025). In summary, lnu(D), lsa(B), 
mph(B), tet(W), tet(T), and tet(Q) all showed negative correlations with 
hydrolytic activity in AD, consistent with the phenomenon that Air-NBW 
enhances hydrolysis. On days 21 and 49, Air-NBW increased the abun­
dance of lnu(H), lnu(B), vat(B), tet(M) and tet(44) (Fig. 3b and 3c). Their 
risk levels were IV, I, IV, II, and III, respectively (Peng et al., 2025; Zhang 
et al., 2021). The risks associated with lnu(H), vat(B) and tet(44) were 
relatively low. Although Air-NBW led to a slight increase in lnu(B), the 
change was minimal. In contrast, tet(M) exhibited an overall decreasing 
trend. In conclusion, while some genes showed an increase in risk, their 
overall impact remained negligible.
On days 21 and 49, the total abundance of MGEs in the NBW group 
was lower than in the control (Fig. 4a). Under mesophilic conditions, 
MN decreased by 30.2% compared with MD, and by 50.7%, respectively. 
In contrast, under psychrotrophic conditions, PN decreased only slightly 
relative to PD, by 1.4% and 2.2%. This decrease coincided with Air- 
NBW-induced shifts in key environmental parameters, including 
higher pH and TAN (Fig. 1a and 1c), and with concurrent changes in 
community composition. In particular, the relative abundances of 
Bacillota and Pseudomonadota, which represent major potential MGE- 
associated hosts in this system, were reduced in the NBW group 
(Fig. 2a) (Flores-Orozco et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2020). 
However, under the psychrotrophic conditions, the strong constraints 
imposed by temperature on microbial metabolism and growth slowed 
community succession, thereby markedly weakening the impact of 
environmental changes, such as pH and TAN, on host populations and 
their associated mobile genetic elements (Dal Bello & Abreu, 2024). The 
relationship between MGE reductions and host bacterial shifts is crucial 
(Figs. S8 and S9). The contributions of individual metagenome- 
assembled genomes bins to the treatment-associated differences in 
total MGE abundance (Air-NBW vs. control) were assessed on days 21 
and 49 (Fig. 4b). The cumulative contribution of the top 10 
metagenome-assembled genomes bins decreased from 1.9 × 10-2 on day 
21 to 7.0 × 10-3 on day 49, compared with a decline from 5.0 × 10-3 to 
4.2 × 10-3 under psychrotrophic conditions. These findings demonstrate 
that the ΔContribution was higher under mesophilic conditions, 
particularly on day 21, and decreased over time under both temperature 
conditions. Therefore, Air-NBW had a more pronounced effect on 
reducing MGEs under mesophilic conditions.
The HGT of ARGs is associated with several key pathways, including 
biofilm formation, antioxidation, DNA repair and recombination, as well 
as the type IV secretion system (T4SS) (Fig. S10) (Peng et al., 2025; Tang 
et al., 2023). Biofilms serve as a critical barrier for microorganisms

primarily composed of polysaccharides, destabilizing the biofilm, 
reducing cell aggregation, and decreasing donor-receptor proximity 
(Kobayashi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024). Specifically, on day 49, MN 
exhibited a 39.6% decrease compared with MD, whereas PN showed 
only a 4.6% decrease relative to PD. Under antibiotic stress, microor­
ganisms may activate antioxidant defense systems to scavenge excess 
ROS, thereby alleviating oxidative DNA damage and limiting ROS- 
mediated HGT of ARGs (Peng et al., 2025). Air-NBW may enhance 
antioxidant activity by expanding the gas–liquid interfacial area, 
boosting dissolved O2 transfer, and stabilizing interfacial charge, 
thereby activating redox-responsive regulation and accelerating ROS 
scavenging (Wang et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2022). On day 49, 
antioxidant-related functional genes were upregulated, with MN 
showing a 24.5% increase compared with MD, whereas PN exhibited a 
relatively minor increase of 0.6% relative to PD (Fig. 4c). DNA damage 
can trigger the SOS response, leading to increased expression of 
recombination and repair genes and potentially enhancing HGT of ARGs 
(Yang et al., 2022). Air-NBW treatment was accompanied by a reduction 
in the expression of genes involved in DNA repair and recombination 
(Fig. 4c). On day 49, MN and PN decreased by 0.3% and 1.2% compared 
with MD and PD, respectively. T4SS efficiently mediates conjugative 
transfer through coordinated action of multiple protein components 
(Tang et al., 2023). The expression levels of T4SS-related functional 
genes in the NBW group were similar to those in the corresponding 
control group (Fig. 4c). Overall, the observed changes in these

3.4. Ecological risks of antibiotic resistance genes
Compared with the IS, ERS were reduced across all treatment groups, 
with further mitigation observed after adding Air-NBW (Fig. 5a). The 
conjugation of ARGs with MGEs may be the core mechanism driving the 
spread of ARGs in AD (Jiao et al., 2024). The co-occurrence level of 
ARGs and MGEs in the NBW group was lower than that in the corre­
sponding control group, indicating reduced mobility (Fig. 5b). On day 
49, MN and PN decreased by 12.7% and 9.7% compared with MD and 
PD, respectively. The NBW group was closer to the origin compared with 
the corresponding control group, indicating that Air-NBW can reduce 
ERS (Rumi et al., 2024). Additionally, the ERS under psychrotrophic 
conditions was lower than that under mesophilic conditions. On day 49, 
PN and PD decreased by 22.2% and 19.4% compared with MN and MD, 
respectively. This may be because, under mesophilic conditions, the 
proportion of drug-resistant bacteria and genetic variability within 
populations increase relative to psychrotrophic conditions, raising the 
probability of drug-resistant mutations occurring (Rodríguez-Verdugo 
et al., 2020). Furthermore, as reservoirs of ARGs, microbial communities 
amplify the effect of temperature on the spread of resistance through 
internal gene transfer (Luo et al., 2025).
In practical applications, AD has been widely adopted for treating 
CM, efficiently degrading organic waste into biogas for energy recovery 
while reducing pollutant emissions (He et al., 2025). As a green additive, 
Air-NBW effectively enhances the system's hydrolysis efficiency and 
methane production without introducing additional contaminants (Bian 
et al., 2026). It also improves digestate quality, enabling treated CM to 
serve as a soil conditioner. This method avoids secondary environmental 
hazards while offering high economic viability, facilitating resource 
recovery, and advancing green, low-carbon agricultural transformation. 
Furthermore, Air-NBW demonstrates potential advantages in controlling 
ARGs, helping reduce overall ERS, particularly under psychrotrophic 
conditions where risk mitigation is more pronounced. Consequently, it is 
well-suited for promotion and application in the potential in high- 
latitude cold regions.
4. Conclusions
Air-NBW enhances methane production from anaerobic digestion of 
cattle manure under both mesophilic and psychrotrophic conditions by 
improving hydrolysis, optimizing microbial communities, and upregu­
lating key functional genes involved in hydrogenotrophic and aceto­
clastic methanogenesis pathways. Air-NBW also reduces the total 
abundance of mobile genetic elements, particularly under mesophilic 
conditions. Furthermore, Air-NBW is associated with changes in the 
expression of functional genes involved in biofilm formation and anti­
oxidant defense, which influence reactive oxygen species levels and, in 
turn, affect the potential for antibiotic resistance genes transfer via 
horizontal gene transfer. Under both mesophilic and psychrotrophic 
conditions, Air-NBW reduced the abundance of lnu(D), lsa(B), and mph 
(B) (MLS) as well as, tet(W), tet(T), and tet(Q) (tetracycline), thereby 
decreasing the total abundance of antibiotic resistance genes. Ulti­
mately, Air-NBW reduced the ecological risk scores of the final digestate, 
with a particularly pronounced effect under psychrotrophic conditions.
